messages.subject: QUARK and MICE
parts:
I am currently attempting to use QUARK in order to then impute a dataset with a large amount of missing data using MICE. In order to practice the script, I pulled 40 variables from the larger dataset. That seemed to work (i.e. I ran descriptives and some CFAs and all was well), so I added 80 more variables from the same initially pulled from dataset to give my script a second check. Now I cannot get a CFA to even converge. I am hoping someone could 1) check my script and 2) give insight as to why the CFAs would run with the first test dataset but not the second test dataset. I know that the datasets are biased, but I would assume CFAs would converge in both. 

set.seed(123321)
library(lavaan)
library(semTools)
quark.list <- quark(data = QUARKtoimpute, id = c(1)) #The ID variable in my dataset is column 1
final.data <- combinequark(quark = quark.list, percent = 80)
imp <- mice(final.data)
completedData <- complete(imp, action="long")

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: QUARK and MICE
parts:
I'm confused.  The script you posted is only about using quark() and imputing the data with mice(). But the problem you described is about fitting a CFA model to data, without specifying whether you are fitting the model to the incomplete data or the imputed data.  I imagine the latter, in which case is there a convergence problem with one or some or all imputed data sets?  Or does the error occur in quark() or mice()? Posting your full script as well as the error would help show exactly where the problem occurs.

From your description, though, convergence problems with an 80-variable model might not be surprising, depending on your sample size and how well your (probably very restrictive) CFA model actually approximates the data-generating process.  A CFA model with simple structure would try to reproduce 80*(80 - 1)/2 = 3160 observed covariances with only 80 factor loadings and only a few factor correlations (assuming you have multiple factors).  You can probably fit such a model to data simulated from that model, but I doubt real data with such large dimensions would conform to such a simple model, and it might take a large sample to even find a "best" set of estimated parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts: Since I initially posted, I reran the mice imputations and now the CFA is running, but the model fit is awful.

That doesn't mean the imputations didn't work.  Try using FIML on the original data and see if you get similar poor fit.  Of course, they might differ because the imputation model contains more (auxiliary) variables, so you could also try including some using auxiliary() in the semTools package to add some auxiliary variables to your model.  If fit looks radically different, then maybe imputations were a bit wonky.
In addition, when running simple correlations the data isn't looking exactly like I would think it would.

Such as?  Take a look at some univariate histograms and bivariate scatterplots of the imputed data to see if there are any crazy outliers, indicating the imputation model needs to be a bit more constrained.
I am most concerned that the imputation script is correct. It runs, but I am not sure if I am leaving anything out that would improve the imputation.
I haven't noticed any problems in your scripts.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: QUARK and MICE
parts: Are these Aux variables reliable to use for imputation?

Not sure.  I have only read one methodological study on this method, using only 8 variables.  It was a good proof of concept, but I'm not sure how well it "scales up" to larger dimensions like you are using -- which is of course the whole benefit of using this method to reduce the dimensionality of auxiliaries.  

Note that you could also just save the columns of principal components that are output in the single imputation.  Save them to your original data set, then use them as auxiliaries in a FIML analysis.  FIML is more efficient than multiple imputation anyway, so it is usually preferable.  Unless you can't use FIML (e.g., with categorical outcomes).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
